beats.say: A queue that makes tickets cost more. And you only see it later.
The first card promises a standing ticket at the opening price.
The second card shows a "standard" ticket with the same seat type but no guarantee of availability.
The third card advertises an "in-demand" ticket that claims you'll get a spot if the show fills up.
The odd part: standing tickets jumped from £148.50 to £355 after hours in line. Looks like a mistake.
Ticketmaster's "in-demand" option updates the price as demand climbs.
While you sit in the online queue, the system records each new purchase and bumps the tag on the waiting tickets.
When you finally click, the higher £355 price appears, and you realize you paid for the surge.
You see it everywhere. A gym lists a basic class, a premium class and a peak-time class priced higher to promise a spot when demand spikes.
A café offers a regular coffee, a limited-edition brew and a rush-hour brew that costs more but guarantees a seat during the busiest hour.
In both cases the higher-priced, "guaranteed-access" option feels smart because it promises entry when you need it most.
If a price climbs while you wait, the increase is the trick. Follow for more.
